domains.title: Seonangshin, the Village Guardian
domains.subtitle: boundary spirit who protects settlements and travellers
domains.lead: Seonangshin is the village guardian spirit who protects settlements, boundaries, and travellers from harm in Korean tradition. The name means "Village spirit" and belongs to the domain "Village Guardian, Boundary." Seonangshin is the spirit who guards the village boundary, usually honoured at a shrine near the entrance to the settlement. The deity is believed to protect the community from epidemics, disasters, war, and wandering malevolent forces.

cards.name: Village Guardian
cards.desc: Seonangshin defends the settlement and its people from harm.

cards.name: Boundary Shrine
cards.desc: The seonangdang marks the threshold between civilised space and the wild.

cards.name: War and Protection
cards.desc: The spirit is invoked against invasion, epidemic, and disaster.

cards.name: Community Rites
cards.desc: Annual dongje festivals renew the bond between village and guardian.

symbols.name: Seonangdang shrine
symbols.meaning: The stacked-stone or open-air shrine at the village entrance, where cultivated ground meets mountain — the physical address of the guardian, recorded in regional folklore surveys across every Korean province.

symbols.name: Geumjul sacred rope
symbols.meaning: The twisted straw rope hung with white paper strips and gourds, which seals a space against pollution and announces that the boundary is under the guardian's watch.

symbols.name: Jangseung and sotdae
symbols.meaning: The carved wooden guardian generals and bird-topped poles that stand sentinel at village paths — the human art of the same threshold the spirit patrols invisibly.

symbols.name: Village tree
symbols.meaning: The great old tree — pine, zelkova, or ginkgo — beside the shrine, believed to be the guardian's dwelling or her resting place between patrols.

mythology.lead: Seonangshin has no epic cycle; her mythology is the living archive of Korean village religion — boundary shrines, communal rites, and origin legends recorded in classical miscellanies such as the Samguk Yusa and the nineteenth-century Dongguk Sesigi, then catalogued by twentieth-century folklore surveys. The narratives vary by region and by shamanic lineage, and the record says so.

myths.title: The Shrine at the Village Gate
myths.text: Every traditional Korean village kept a seonangdang, a small open shrine set where the settlement's paths met the fields — the precise point where cultivated space gave way to mountain and wild. The nineteenth-century miscellany Dongguk Sesigi (1849) describes the offerings made there: rice wine poured out, lengths of cloth hung, the season's first fruits presented, and prayers spoken to keep epidemic and disaster outside the settlement. The shrine was usually nothing grand — a ring of stones, a low platform, sometimes a great guardian tree under which the spirit was thought to rest — but its placement was theology: the village existed because someone stood watch at its edge. The offerings were not thanks so much as a retainer's wages: the community fed its sentinel so the sentinel would keep the boundary sealed. The myth's meaning is spatial — a people defines itself by what it places at its border.

myths.title: Guardian of the Threshold
myths.text: Korean village religion builds its boundary in visible grammar: the geumjul, a twisted straw rope hung with paper strips and dried gourds, declares sacred space; the jangseung, grinning wooden posts carved in the likeness of generals, stand sentinel at the paths; the sotdae, tall poles topped with carved birds, lift the village's wishes skyward. Seonangshin was imagined moving among these markers as a patrolling official or armed warrior, inspecting the fence between the human world and the wilderness. Travellers passing the shrine dismounted, bowed, or left a pinch of food; to pass carelessly was to risk misfortune on the road, for the guardian noted disrespect as readily as reverence. Twentieth-century folklore surveys recorded the custom still alive in remote villages, and the road-customs around surviving seonangdang preserve it as etiquette. The threshold is the myth itself: safety is a negotiated privilege, renewed at every crossing, and the boundary stone is the signature on the treaty.

myths.title: The Maiden Who Guards the Gate
myths.text: Korean folklore preserves a recurring origin legend for its village guardians: the seonangshin is the spirit of a young woman — often a maiden who died unmarried — who took up the guardianship of the settlement that failed her in life. The motif is catalogued in the National Folk Museum of Korea's Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015) and across the regional legend collections, and it belongs to the wider family of Korean shrine legends in which the wronged dead become protective powers when honoured and dangerous ones when neglected. Versions attach the guardian to a particular tree, stone, or spring; some name her; many were collected from shamans whose village rituals address her by title rather than by name. The sources disagree on details by region — Jeju, the mainland south, and the central provinces each keep their own telling — but the structural claim is stable: the guardian was once one of the community's own, and her watch is the settlement's debt made visible. The legend reads marginality transformed into sovereignty: the figure with least power in life becomes the power that rules the boundary.

myths.title: The Dongje Festival
myths.text: Once a year — most often in the first lunar month — the village gathered at the seonangdang for the dongje, the communal rite that renewed the covenant between settlement and guardian. A ritual specialist, and in many regions a shaman, led the prayers; offerings of food, wine, and in earlier centuries a pig were presented; and the rite closed with shared food and drink, the boundary between household and community briefly dissolved. The point was as social as it was sacred: the dongje synchronized the village calendar, settled obligations, and reasserted that protection was a collective undertaking, not a private charm. The great surviving example is Hahoe village's byeolsingut kut, a masked shamanic rite still performed for the settlement's tutelary powers and honoured by UNESCO; the National Folk Museum's surveys record dozens of humbler dongje across the peninsula. Where a seonangdang has been restored as heritage, the rite often returns as festival — the same gathering under a new description. The rite performs the community's oldest claim: together, watched over, we persist.

etymology.derivation: The Hanja 城隍神 means "city wall and moat spirit," the guardian deity of a fortified settlement. In Korean reading it becomes Seonghwangsin, but the folk pronunciation Seonangshin is widely used in village cults.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Seonangshin, the Hangul form is 서낭신 and the Hanja form is 城隍神. Hangul ‘서낭신’ and Hanja ‘城隍神’ (Seonghwangsin in Sino-Korean reading); the figure is also called Dongbaek Seonang or Dodangsin in regional cults. The ASCII form seonangshin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Seonangshin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Seonangshin sits at the intersection of indigenous Korean village guardian cults and the Sino-Korean city-god tradition: the Hanja 城隍 name the Chinese Chénghuáng, whose cult the Tang and Ming ritual canons regulated as a tutelary of walled cities, and Joseon-period Confucian administration licensed official seonghwang shrines with state sacrifices while village religion continued the older rites at the seonangdang. The figure also overlaps with neighbouring powers: in mountain villages she is easily conflated with the mountain god Sanshin, and generals who defended a region were sometimes posthumously honoured as seonangshin, merging hero cult with boundary cult. Buddhist temples absorbed village shrines in some regions, giving the guardian a bodhisattva's halo without erasing her office. The result is a layered deity: Confucian official, shamanic sentinel, and honoured ancestor in one — a fusion typical of Korean religious history, where traditions rarely replace one another and almost always share the gate.
lore.culturalLegacy: Seonangshin remains visible in the Korean cultural landscape: guardian trees, stone cairns, jangseung posts, and restored seonangdang shrines stand in heritage villages such as Hahoe and Yangdong, inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2010, and on Jeju the island's stone seonangdang cairns are protected as folk heritage. Urban Korea keeps the learned cousin of the cult alive in seonghwang shrines, and the dongje survives wherever a village still gathers — as rite, as festival, or as tourist calendar. The figure also informs Korean ideas of community, boundary, and collective responsibility: to share in the guardian's upkeep is to remain a member of the settlement. In recent decades Seonangshin has even been invoked metaphorically in discussions of online community safety and the guardianship of shared digital spaces — the old sentinel posted at a new kind of gate.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Seonangshin invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. Her shrine stands exactly where the map of the human world ends: beyond it, path becomes trail, field becomes mountain, and the names of things grow thin. Every settled people has needed such a figure — a watcher whose jurisdiction is the border itself — and Korea gave the office a name worth restoring. The seonangdang asks a question that cities still answer badly: who guards the threshold, and who pays the keeper?

The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition. It marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names. A village spirit may seem a modest subject for a temple, but guardianship of shared space is among the oldest religious offices there is — older than scripture, older than empire. To name Seonangshin truly is to acknowledge that every community, digital or ancestral, survives by the same covenant: something watches the gate, and the gate holds because it is honoured.

lore.archaeology: Seonangshin's material witnesses are standing, not buried. The UNESCO-listed clan villages Hahoe (Andong) and Yangdong (Gyeongju) preserve their guardian shrines, village trees, and ritual topography intact; Jeju's stone seonangdang — low cairns of stacked volcanic rock with a single sacred pole — survive by the hundreds across the island and are documented in provincial folk-heritage registers. The National Folk Museum of Korea's regional surveys record seonangdang structures, jangseung pairs, and sotdae poles from every province, many photographed before the mid-twentieth century upheavals. Documentary witnesses complement the fabric: the Dongguk Sesigi (1849) describes the rites, and Joseon administrative records list licensed seonghwang shrines. No excavation is required; the cult's archaeology is the vernacular landscape itself.
